# computational-paradigms

A comparative study of computational models. The study asks:

> **How do different computational models represent, retain and resolve
> partially specified computations?**

The same sixteen problems are posed to each system, most of them in stages. A stage
adds information, or in a few problems replaces or withdraws it. The study
records:

- what each system reports;
- what it keeps waiting;
- what it has to redo;
- how much control code, supporting code and manual help it needs.

The method follows TPK (Knuth and Trabb Pardo, 1976), which wrote one fixed
problem in each language's own idiom. Here there is a fixed set of
problems, incremental and symbolic rather than numerical. The aim is a map
of trade-offs, not a ranking.

## Status

**Draft 0.6, the freeze candidate. No system has been compared.**

- Draft 0.1 was reviewed independently. Draft 0.2 answered every finding
  ([`reviews/review-1.md`](reviews/review-1.md)). Draft 0.3 applied the
  decisions on its open questions
  ([`reviews/decisions-0.2.md`](reviews/decisions-0.2.md)). A second,
  fresh review of draft 0.3 was answered in draft 0.4
  ([`reviews/review-2.md`](reviews/review-2.md)), and the decisions on it
  in draft 0.5 ([`reviews/decisions-0.4.md`](reviews/decisions-0.4.md)).
  A third review, of draft 0.5, is answered in draft 0.6
  ([`reviews/review-3.md`](reviews/review-3.md)). Draft 0.7 is the freeze
  candidate: it fixes the pins ([`PINS.md`](PINS.md)), the ALGOL 60 step,
  the assessment of hidden variants, and three clarifications from the
  held-out check.
- The classification rules have been calibrated on P03 and P13 in all four
  systems, by two independent classifiers
  ([`calibration/`](calibration)), and checked on a held-out problem, P02
  in Python and ALGOL 60 ([`calibration/held-out/`](calibration/held-out)).
  The calibration programs are development examples, not results.
- Nothing is frozen.
- No programs have been written for this study.

Programs come after the freeze (`PROTOCOL.md`).

## Contents

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| [`SPECIFICATION.md`](SPECIFICATION.md) | the question, the conventions, the classes of outcome, and what is not assumed |
| [`problems/`](problems) | the sixteen problems, in mathematical notation, with their valid outcomes |
| [`METRICS.md`](METRICS.md) | what is measured, and the frozen rules for classing tokens |
| [`PROTOCOL.md`](PROTOCOL.md) | phases, amendments, evidence classes, configurations, how programs are written, run and recorded |
| [`AMENDMENTS.md`](AMENDMENTS.md) | the numbered changes since the freeze (`spec-1.0.1`) |
| [`PINS.md`](PINS.md) | the version or commit of every system, fixed at the freeze |
| [`systems/`](systems) | each system's configurations and evidence class |
| [`calibration/`](calibration) | the checks of the classification rules: development examples, not results |
| [`variants/`](variants) | the sealed hidden variants, one set per wave |
| [`tools/`](tools) | the hygiene check, and the script that seals the variants |
| [`sources/`](sources) | where the problems and the systems' idioms come from |
| [`reviews/`](reviews) | the reviews of each draft, and the response to every finding |
| [`results/`](results) | empty until the freeze |

## Systems

The first comparison is of four:

- [Absys](systems/absys), reconstructed;
- [SWI-Prolog](systems/swi-prolog), modern;
- [Python](systems/python), the modern imperative baseline;
- [ALGOL 60](systems/algol-60), the historical imperative baseline.

Each has the configurations described in its folder. Earlier experiments on Absys and SWI-Prolog are in
the [absys](https://github.com/chrishayuk/absys) repository. They are not
results of this study: they were written before the problems were fixed.

Proposed after them, in order, and not started:

- PLANNER, with the described language and Micro-Planner kept separate;
- Conniver;
- Concurrent Prolog;
- concurrent constraint programming;
- Oz.

These are a sequence for comparison, not a claim that each influenced the
next.

## Licence

Apache-2.0.
# Specification

*Draft 0.7, 27 November 2026. Not frozen; the freeze candidate. Draft 0.1 was reviewed
independently; the findings and the response to each are in
[`reviews/`](reviews). Draft 0.3 added the decisions taken on draft 0.2
(`reviews/decisions-0.2.md`). Draft 0.4 answered the second review, of
draft 0.3 (`reviews/review-2.md`). Draft 0.5 applied the decisions on
draft 0.4 (`reviews/decisions-0.4.md`). Draft 0.6 answers the third review
(`reviews/review-3.md`). See `PROTOCOL.md` for how the specification is
frozen.*

## The question

**How do different computational models represent, retain and resolve
partially specified computations?**

A computation is *partially specified* when the information it needs has not
all arrived. Some of its unknowns have no value yet, some of its relations
have no definition yet, or some of its alternatives cannot yet be told
apart. This study poses the same partially specified problems to several
systems and records what each does with them.

The results are meant to map trade-offs along six dimensions of design, not
to rank systems:

| dimension | what it covers | problems that bear most on it |
|---|---|---|
| **information** | how incomplete knowledge is represented | P01, P02, P06, P07, P16 |
| **execution** | how computations become runnable: order, scheduling, suspension, resumption | P02, P04, P08, P13 |
| **state** | how information changes over time | P10, P14 |
| **search** | how alternatives are explored and retained | P03, P04, P05, P12 |
| **coordination** | how computations communicate and cooperate | P09, P14, P15, P16 |
| **commitment** | how tentative results become final, and irreversible actions | P11, P15 |

**Resources** cut across all six: retained state, recomputation, control
code, supporting code and intervention. Each metric in `METRICS.md` names
the dimension it measures, or resources.

## What this specification does not assume

None of the following is taken as true. Each is a question the results may
bear on:

- that declarative computation is better than imperative computation;
- that a fair search is better than a depth-first one;
- that suspending a computation is better than restarting it;
- that keeping alternatives alive is better than backtracking;
- that less explicit control code makes a better programming model;
- that information only ever accumulates. Some problems replace or
  retract information (P10).

Each design may have advantages under different limits of memory, time or
implementation effort.

## The problems

| | problem | what it probes |
|---|---|---|
| P01 | [unknown equality](problems/01-unknown-equality.md) | how a relation between unknowns is represented |
| P02 | [late information](problems/02-late-information.md) | whether a computation resumes when information arrives |
| P03 | [reversible relations](problems/03-reversible-relations.md) | whether one definition serves several directions |
| P04 | [unbounded alternative](problems/04-unbounded-alternative.md) | whether an endless alternative hides a finite one, in either order |
| P05 | [late contradiction](problems/05-late-contradiction.md) | how alternatives are kept and dropped as constraints arrive |
| P06 | [negation](problems/06-negation.md) | whether negation is sound while its unknowns are unknown |
| P07 | [simultaneous constraints](problems/07-simultaneous-constraints.md) | which sets of equations are solved, and how |
| P08 | [late definition](problems/08-late-definition.md) | what an application of a relation not yet defined means and does |
| P09 | [concurrent goals](problems/09-concurrent-goals.md) | independent computations, and computations that share information |
| P10 | [state replacement](problems/10-state-replacement.md) | values that change, relations that keep holding, information withdrawn |
| P11 | [irreversible effects](problems/11-irreversible-effects.md) | whether external actions are tied to committed outcomes |
| P12 | [large alternative space](problems/12-large-alternative-space.md) | the time and store of each search strategy |
| P13 | [deterministic scale](problems/13-deterministic-scale.md) | how bookkeeping grows with size, apart from search |
| P14 | [message stream](problems/14-message-stream.md) | a persistent process with state, answering between messages |
| P15 | [merge and committed choice](problems/15-merge-and-committed-choice.md) | interleaving, fairness and arbitration of a resource |
| P16 | [shared information at scale](problems/16-shared-information.md) | propagation, contributors, localised updates and contradiction in a large structure of relations |

The problems are stated in mathematical notation only. A definition's
numbered cases describe a relation; they are not a program, and a program
may express them in whatever form its language uses.

## How a problem is stated

Each problem file gives:

1. **Vocabulary.** The relations, with a definition by cases for every
   relation the problem uses that is not primitive.
2. **Stages.** The information initially available (stage 1), and each
   later piece of information, in the order it arrives. A problem of one
   stage is a query.
3. **Presentation order.** Where a definition or a conjunction has parts,
   the order in which they are written. Some systems' behaviour depends on
   it, so it is part of the problem. A program that changes it is
   *reformulated* (`METRICS.md`).
4. **Valid outcomes.** After every stage, the set of solutions that the
   information so far admits, under the semantics below and any reading the
   problem names.
5. **Observations.** What to record, beyond the common observations below.

## Conventions

### Values and names

- **Values** are integers, atoms and finite sequences of values.
- **Atoms** are written in small capitals, as ᴀ, ʙʀᴏᴡɴ, ᴄ101. In plain
  text they may be written with a leading quote: 'a, 'brown, 'c101.
- ⟨⟩ is the empty sequence, ⟨1,2⟩ a sequence of two, and a ++ b the
  sequence a followed by b. ++ is defined only on sequences.
- **Unknowns** are written in italic lower case where the format allows,
  and are never the same letters as an atom or a relation in the same
  problem. An unknown ranges over all values unless its problem says
  otherwise. Where a relation's case says "for every sequence b", b ranges
  over sequences only.
- **Relations** are written in lower case words: conc, rev, mem.

### Definitions

- A definition is a list of numbered cases. Each is a fact or an
  implication "r(…) if …", whose conjuncts are joined by *and* in the order
  written.
- A definition with no negation is read as the **least relation**
  satisfying its cases.
- A definition with negation is read under the **stratified** (perfect
  model) semantics. Negation is applied only to relations defined at a lower
  stratum, as every definition in this suite does.
- Where a problem says a relation is given by facts in a **closed world**,
  only the stated facts are true.
- Some problems also name a second reading, such as a stream reading over
  infinite sequences. There, the problem gives valid outcomes under each
  reading, and a result is classified under each separately.

### Arithmetic and comparison

The primitive vocabulary is +, −, · on integers, written as relations
(a + b = c holds of three integers; any place may be unknown), and the
comparisons =, ≠, <, ≤, >, ≥. Comparisons other than = and ≠ hold only of
integers. A compound expression such as x + y + z = 12 abbreviates a
conjunction of primitive relations with fresh unknowns. Writing it either
way, compound or decomposed, is a transcription of the problem
(`METRICS.md`, class P).

## Stages and monotonicity

A stage adds information to what came before it, unless the problem marks it
as **replacing** (a named quantity takes a new value) or **retracting**
(information given earlier is withdrawn), as P10 does. Two monotonicities
are distinguished:

- **Information monotonicity.** The stated information only grows. This
  holds in every problem except those that say they replace or retract.
- **Conclusion monotonicity.** Every conclusion a system reports stays
  valid once later information arrives. This does not follow from the first.
  Under a closed world, adding a definition or a fact can make a conclusion
  that was valid (no solutions; a negation true) invalid at the next stage.

The valid outcomes after stage k are always computed from the whole of the
information of stages 1 to k, under the problem's readings. Where they
contradict a valid outcome of an earlier stage, the problem file says so.
Each result records every reported conclusion that a later stage withdrew,
and how the system showed the withdrawal, if it did.

## Outcomes

Each stage of each run is classified on three axes, recorded separately,
and on a fourth, effects, in P11 only. A residual representation also
records its simplification (below).

Separately from the axes, **expressibility** is recorded once per
configuration and sub-problem (for a relation used in several directions,
once per direction), by one rule for every system:

| expressibility | meaning | the program of record |
|---|---|---|
| **expressible** | the problem's definitions can be transcribed | the transcription |
| **expressible with reformulation** | it cannot be transcribed, but a reformulation keeps the relation's meaning on every input the problem and its hidden variants use | the reformulation, with its R tokens counted |
| **not expressible** | only a reformulation that changes the meaning (dropping a guard the inputs depend on, for instance), or supporting code, can be written | none. Any such reformulation is run and reported as a named variant |

Both the classification and any named variant are always reported. That a
reformulation was needed is itself a result.

### 1. Semantic result

Judged on the set of solutions the report denotes, compared with the valid
outcomes.

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| **complete** | the report denotes exactly the valid outcomes. Whether an empty set was reported as empty is recorded by simplification (*inconsistency undetected*) and by answer completeness |
| **partial** | the report denotes a nonempty proper subset of the valid outcomes. This includes a representation that drops solutions, such as a solver that restricts an unknown to integers when the problem lets it range wider |
| **unsound** | the report denotes an outcome that is not valid, or reports that there are none where valid outcomes exist |
| **undetermined** | the report consists of conditions whose equivalence to the valid outcomes the classifiers cannot establish |
| **none reported** | nothing was reported |

A system that reports one answer of several, for a query that asks for one
(*any one* queries, in later problems), is *complete* for that query.

**Correctness and simplification are kept apart.** A residual that is
equivalent to the valid outcomes is *complete*, however unreduced. How far
the system reduced it is recorded separately, as **simplification**:

| simplification | meaning |
|---|---|
| **reduced** | no smaller equivalent representation exists |
| **reducible** | a smaller equivalent representation exists, which the system did not reach |
| **inconsistency undetected** | the conditions denote the empty set, and the system has not reported that there are none |

One representation is smaller than another if it has fewer relations left
to decide, or the same number with fewer occurrences of unknowns. So:

- P02, stage 1: u + v = 16, held, is *complete* / *residual* / *reduced*.
- P07c: x + y = 10, held, is *complete* / *residual* / *reduced*.
- P07b: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, held, is *complete* / *residual* /
  *reducible*, since x = 7, y = 3 is smaller.
- P07f: x + y = 10 and x + y = 11, held, is *complete* / *residual* /
  *inconsistency undetected*.

So a system that does nothing with a set of relations it cannot solve is
not marked wrong. Its simplification shows what it left undone, and is
compared alongside the semantic result.

A binding that the system holds is **reported** if the harness's
`observe()` can read it at the end of the stage, including at the moment
a budget runs out, whether or not the system's mechanism for answers
would deliver it (P09d2, P15b). The one exception is P09d1, whose finite
reading has no solution: there, a binding held while the producer still
runs is recorded as an observation, and the result is *none reported*.

### 2. Representation

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| **explicit** | each solution is given as values |
| **solved form** | each unknown is either bound to a term built from values, unknowns, ⟨⟩ and ++, or free, or identified with another unknown, and no relation remains to be decided |
| **residual** | some relations remain to be decided. The residual conditions are recorded, with their size beside the size of the input |
| **cyclic** | a term that is not finite (a rational tree), presented as such |

Whether a residual is equivalent to the valid outcomes is checked by the
classifiers (`PROTOCOL.md`, Roles), by hand or by a published checking
script, with the reasoning recorded. Sizes of representations are measured
on the primitive decomposition (`Conventions`).

Where a program reports a stage in two forms (the relations it holds, and
the solutions it derived from them, for instance), the representation is
classified on the more explicit form that is valid, and the other is
recorded as an observation. A form derived by reformulation keeps its R
tokens. *(Clarified after the held-out check.)*

A residual counts as reported only if it is state that the system or the
program holds and acts on at a later stage, read by `observe()`. Printing
the posed information back is not a report. Beside simplification, a flag
records a residual **identical to the posed information**, so that a
system that held the relations and did nothing yet can be told apart from
one that transformed them.

### 3. Execution state

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| **finished** | the system has stopped and holds no more work for this stage |
| **alternatives pending** | the system has stopped after an answer, and holds alternatives that a request for more answers would resume |
| **suspended** | the system has stopped, and holds work that later information may resume |
| **budget** | the step budget ran out (`PROTOCOL.md`). Nontermination is presumed, not proved |
| **timeout** | the harness's safety limit on time ran out before the budget did. The run is rerun once with the limit raised (`PROTOCOL.md`). Answers reported before the limit are classified on the semantic axis |
| **error** | the system stopped with an error, recorded verbatim |

A run may be both *alternatives pending* and *suspended*. Both are
recorded.

### 4. Effects

Only for problems with external effects (P11), a fourth axis
records whether the effects performed match the outcome committed to. P11
defines it.

## Observations common to every problem

After each stage, record:

1. the outcomes reported, verbatim, collected as `PROTOCOL.md` says;
2. the three classifications above;
3. how the unknowns that remain unknown are represented;
4. the alternatives the system holds, and whether they are all live at once
   or kept for backtracking, in the unit its systems file defines;
5. what the system holds as suspended or waiting work, in its own terms,
   and how many items;
6. the metrics of `METRICS.md` that apply to a stage;
7. any conclusion reported at an earlier stage that this stage withdrew;
8. any manual action needed to pose the stage.

## Disclosure: where the problems came from

P01–P08 were first run, in other forms, on a reconstruction of Absys
(1967–68), and most were chosen because Absys did something notable with
them. The reconstruction itself was developed while those experiments ran,
and some of its decisions were taken because of them
(`systems/absys/README.md`). The suite may therefore favour systems that
resemble Absys. Disclosure does not remove that, so:

- P07 includes cases that Absys is known or expected to handle badly.
- P10–P16 were added after review: state replacement, effects, large
  search spaces, scale, persistent processes, arbitration, and shared
  information at scale. These are
  problems where imperative, backtracking and concurrent designs are
  expected to do well, and Absys may do badly or not at all.
- The first comparison includes two imperative baselines (Python and
  ALGOL 60), so that the suite is not only a comparison of declarative
  systems.
- Retained state and recomputation are measured as costs. Each system's
  store is measured in its own units, which are not comparable. What is
  compared across systems is the **problem-defined quantities**, such as
  the alternatives a problem's own terms say are held, and the **growth
  exponent** of each system's store and steps as a problem's size grows

52	| role | does | has access to |

81	## Evidence classification
82	
83	Every implementation is given one or more of these classes:
84	
85	| class | meaning |
86	|---|---|
87	| **original** | a surviving historical implementation, on the hardware or software it was written for |
88	| **rehosted** | a surviving historical implementation, running in a modern environment (an emulator, a port of the original source) |
89	| **reconstructed** | a modern implementation derived from historical documents, where no implementation survives |
90	| **modern** | a contemporary implementation of the language |
91	| **extended** | mechanisms supplied for the experiment, beyond the implementation's own |
92	
93	Two qualifiers may be attached to a class:
94	
95	- *with external mechanisms*: libraries or run-time features outside the
96	  configuration's core are used (`METRICS.md`);
97	- *alternative reading*: a reconstruction run with a decision taken the
98	  other way, where its sources conflict.
99	
100	Results are always reported with the class. No result from a modern or
101	extended configuration is attributed to the historical language. Where a
102	language was described more fully than it was implemented (PLANNER and
103	Micro-Planner, for instance), the described language and the implemented
104	subset are separate systems.
105	
106	## Configurations
107	
108	A configuration is one system with a stated set of mechanisms. Results are
109	kept separate per configuration, so that a capability introduced later is
110	not attributed to the earlier model. Each systems file lists, per
111	configuration:
112	
113	- its core, built-in by built-in;
114	- its flags;
115	- the unit of steps, of an alternative and of store, and how each is
116	  measured;
117	- what "the same computation" means. That is, whether a stage can be
118	  received into a computation already running, and how.
119	
120	A reconstruction is pinned at a commit when the specification is frozen.
121	Any later change to it, for whatever reason, makes a new configuration,
122	reported separately, and never replaces the pinned one.
123	
124	## Instrumentation
125	
126	A measurement added to a system must not change what it computes. For a
127	reconstruction:
128	
129	- the unmodified commit is kept as the baseline;
130	- instrumentation is made on a separate branch, and recorded as its own
131	  commit;
132	- it may not change scheduling, search, equality, suspension or any other
133	  rule of the machine;
134	- the instrumented build, with measurement on and off, must give output
135	  identical to the baseline's, byte for byte, on every example and in every
136	  output mode, including full traces. The check and its result are
137	  recorded.

139	## The harness interface
140	
141	Every harness provides exactly these operations, and nothing that orders,
142	chooses or re-poses goals on its own:
143	
144	- **pose(stage)**: give the system the information of one stage, into the
145	  same computation if the configuration allows it, or else by reposing.
146	  A reposed run replays **every** stage 1 to k in order, replacements and
147	  withdrawals included, and the program must carry them out. The harness
148	  never works out the net information itself;
149	- **spawn(computation)**: start a separate computation in the same
150	  instance (P09), returning at once where the configuration can run
151	  computations side by side. In a configuration that cannot, the first
152	  runs to its end or its budget, and then the next;
153	- **answers(cap)**: collect the answers the system reports, through its
154	  standard mechanism for enumerating them, until it is exhausted, the
155	  budget runs out, or `cap` answers have been collected. `cap` is 1 for an
156	  *any one* query and 20 otherwise, as each problem states. The execution
157	  state is classified after the call;
158	- **observe()**: record the state the common observations need, including
159	  bindings the system holds (`SPECIFICATION.md`, "reported");
160	- **print()**.
161	
162	Each system's systems file says what its standard mechanism for answers
163	is. For Python and ALGOL 60, it is the values the program prints.
164	
165	**Observing must not consume the computation.** In a system where
166	collecting answers would end or alter the computation that the next stage
167	extends (exhausting a backtracking search, for instance), the observation
168	of stage k is taken on a separate run of stages 1 to k. The incremental
169	run is left as it was.
170	
171	**Commitments are preserved when a run is reposed.** When a commit stage
172	has selected an outcome v (P11), a reposed run replays it as the
173	information x = v. It does not ask the system to select again, which could
174	commit to a different outcome.
175	
176	**External effects** (P11) are written to one log per problem, never reset,
177	across every run the harness makes for classification, reposed runs
178	included. Separate observation runs write to a separate log, which is not
179	judged. Entries that are duplicated only because a run was reposed are
180	counted separately, as the cost of reposing an irreversible effect.
181	
182	Concurrency used to run computations (threads, processes) is a mechanism of
183	the configuration, listed in its systems file. A harness may not run
184	computations concurrently itself. In P09, all computations run in one
185	instance of the system, sharing one database, never in separate operating
186	system processes.

188	## Writing a program
189	
190	1. Write it from the problem file. Programs written for this study's
191	   precursors (the absys experiments E01–E09) exist, and their author may
192	   have seen them; each program says whether its author had.
193	2. Use the idioms of the system's period where they are known. Cite the
194	   source of each idiom: a manual, a paper or a published program.
195	3. Transcribe the definitions given. Anything else is reformulation, and
196	   counts as R.
197	4. Where several idiomatic programs are possible, choose one per
198	   configuration and problem before any is run, or run and report every
199	   variant. In either case, one is designated the **primary** variant
200	   before any is run, and stands for the configuration.
201	5. **No anticipation.** The code that handles stage k may not depend on the
202	   content of any later stage.
203	6. **Genericity.** A program must stay correct when the constants in a
204	   problem's stages are changed. It keeps them in one marked place, or reads
205	   them as input, so that the verifier can substitute them. Each problem
206	   has hidden variants with other constants, held by someone who does not
207	   write programs. Every program is run on them after its results are
208	   recorded. The custodian works out each variant's valid outcomes
209	   independently, stage by stage, as the problem files give them for the
210	   original constants. A variant's outcomes need not have the same classes
211	   as the original's: other constants can make a finite outcome infinite,
212	   or a consistent stage inconsistent. A program's run on a variant is
213	   classified against **that variant's** valid outcomes, on the semantic and
214	   effects axes, exactly as a primary run is. A program **fails** a variant
215	   where that classification differs from its classification on the
216	   original constants, each against its own valid outcomes: a program
217	   complete on the original and unsound on the variant fails it. It is
218	   recorded as such, since it encodes a conclusion rather than computing
219	   it. The custodian records, for each variant, which of the original's
220	   outcome classes it was built to keep, if any.
221	7. A program may not be revised after its results are seen, except to fix a
222	   transcription error: a place where the program departs from the text of
223	   the problem file. Each fix is recorded as a diff, with the reason. A
224	   program changed for any other reason is a separate, named variant, and
225	   is reported as such.
226	8. Record the author of each program, human or agent.
227	
228	## Running
229	
230	- Pin the version of every system, and record its source and commit.
231	- **Budget.** 10⁶ steps in the system's own unit, per stage and per
232	  computation. In P09, each separate computation has its own budget and its
233	  own classification. A reposed run of stages 1 to k has a budget of its
234	  measured restart cost plus 10⁶.
235	- **The budget is relative to each system.** 10⁶ Absys steps, SWI-Prolog
236	  inferences and Python instructions are different amounts of work. So
237	  *budget* is a classification within a system, and is not compared
238	  across systems. Each system records, as a calibration figure, its steps
239	  for P13b at n = 10³, or, where P13b is not expressible, for P03e.
240	- **After budget.** If stage k ends in *budget* and the configuration can
241	  keep its computation and continue it, stage k+1 is posed into that same
242	  computation, with a new budget. Whether it can is recorded, since
243	  continuing past an exhausted budget is itself a capability. Stages 1 to
244	  k+1 are reposed only when the configuration cannot continue, and the
245	  reposing counts under restart cost.
246	- **After error.** Stage k+1 is posed by reposing stages 1 to k+1, counted
247	  under restart cost.
248	- **Safety limit.** A limit of 60 seconds per stage protects the harness.
249	  It is not a measurement. A stage it stops is rerun once, with the limit
250	  raised tenfold. If the rerun also stops, *timeout* is final for that
251	  stage. Both runs are recorded. Answers reported before the limit stopped
252	  the run are kept and classified on the semantic axis; only the execution
253	  state is *timeout*.
254	
255	## Modes of running
256	
257	Each program is run in up to three modes:
258	
259	| mode | what it establishes | instrumentation |
260	|---|---|---|
261	| **behaviour** | the outcomes, the three axes and effects | none beyond the harness |
262	| **cost** | steps, answer latency, problem-defined operation counts | step counting only |
263	| **storage** | store, retained alternatives, suspended state | the systems file's storage measurement |
264	
265	- The semantic result and execution state are taken from the behaviour run.
266	- Where two modes can be compared, their semantic results must agree, and
267	  any disagreement is reported as a fault of the instrumentation.
268	- A sampled measurement is never taken from the run that gives the step
269	  count or the classification, because sampling adds steps of its own.
270	- A run that hits the safety limit only because it is instrumented (in
271	  cost or storage mode, when the behaviour run finished) is not evidence
272	  that the model cannot complete the problem. It is recorded as a limit of
273	  the measurement.
274	- Run in CI where the system allows it, and compare with recorded output.

278	Each result is a file `results/<system>/<configuration>/<problem>.md` that

296	- The reasons for choosing a problem, and the history of each system's

424	# Metrics
425	
426	*Draft 0.7. The classification rules below are frozen with the specification,
427	before any system is compared.*
428	
429	Every metric is recorded per system, per configuration, per problem, and per
430	stage where it applies. Raw counts are kept beside every derived figure.
431	Counts in a system's own unit are compared within that system: across
432	stages, configurations and problems, not across systems. Across systems,
433	the comparable figures are the classifications, the qualitative
434	observations, the problem-defined quantities and growth below, and C and R
435	tokens taken relative to P tokens. S is reported apart, per mechanism
436	(rule 12).
437	
438	## The metrics
439	
440	| metric | dimension | definition |
441	|---|---|---|
442	| **problem tokens** | resources | tokens expressing the problem (class P below) |
443	| **control tokens** | execution | tokens specifying order, scheduling, suspension or search (class C) |
444	| **reformulation** | resources | tokens of definitions or arguments the problem does not give, and parts moved from the presentation order (class R) |
445	| **supporting code** | resources | code that provides a mechanism the configuration lacks (class S), counted once per mechanism per configuration, with the problems that use it listed |
446	| **external mechanisms** | resources | libraries, run-time features and extensions used beyond the core of the configuration, listed by name |
447	| **answer completeness** | information, search | see below |
448	| **answer latency** | execution | steps to the first valid answer, steps between successive answers, and steps to the end of the stage |
449	| **suspended state** | execution | unresolved computations held, at each stage boundary and at their peak during the stage, in the system's terms, with a count |
450	| **retained alternatives** | search | alternatives held, at each answer, at each stage boundary, when the budget runs out, and at their peak, in the unit the systems file defines |
451	| **peak store** | resources | the store the computation holds during the stage, as a vector of quantities the systems file defines, each with its current value at the stage boundary and its peak during the stage. Where a true peak cannot be measured, the sampled maximum is reported and labelled as such |
452	| **restart cost** | resources | for a system that cannot receive a stage into its existing computation: the steps of reposing stages 1 to k−1 |
453	| **repeated work** | resources | work done again inside one computation after new information: relations examined again, goals re-solved, name parameters re-evaluated. Each systems file names its source for the count, or says it is not measured |
454	| **problem operations** | resources | applications of each case of each relation the problem defines, counted in the problem's own terms (below). Comparable across systems |
455	| **problem-defined alternatives** | search | alternatives held, in the problem's own terms (below). Comparable across systems |
456	| **intervention** | resources | manual actions needed to make progress (see below) |
457	| **effects** | commitment | P11's effects class, and when each effect was performed |
458	| **coordination** | coordination | in P09, P14 and P15: whether computations progressed independently, what they waited on, and how arbitration was decided |

460	### Answer completeness
461	
462	- Where the valid outcomes are finite and nonempty: valid answers obtained,
463	  over valid answers expected, with the count of invalid answers obtained
464	  beside it.
465	- Where they are empty: whether the system reported that there are none
466	  (yes or no).
467	- Where they are infinite: whether a finite representation equivalent to
468	  them was given (yes or no), and the answers obtained before the budget or
469	  the cap (`PROTOCOL.md`), listed.
470	
471	## Tokens
472	
473	A token is a lexical token of the language, as its own grammar defines it:
474	an identifier, a literal, an operator, a punctuation mark or a keyword.
475	Comments, whitespace and layout are not counted. Where layout is part of the
476	syntax (indentation, line ends), each significant layout element counts as
477	one token.
478	
479	### Classing by construct
480	
481	Tokens are classed by the construct they belong to, not one by one. A
482	construct is the smallest unit with a role in the program: a clause, a
483	goal, a declaration, a definition case, an argument. Every token of a
484	construct takes the construct's class, including its punctuation.
485	
486	| class | what it covers |
487	|---|---|
488	| **P, problem** | the vocabulary and definitions as the problem file gives them; the information of each stage; the connectives that express them (conjunction, disjunction, negation, equality, arithmetic, comparison); the query |
489	| **C, control** | constructs that decide when or in what order: delay and key declarations, coroutine and freeze calls, cuts, tabling declarations, search and labelling directives, generators of values the problem does not state (between/3, for instance), explicit scheduling, priority or fairness annotations, engine and thread calls |
490	| **R, reformulation** | definitions, cases and extra arguments the problem file does not give (an accumulator, for instance); a relation computed in one chosen direction where the problem states it as a relation |
491	| **S, supporting** | code that implements a mechanism the configuration lacks: a meta-interpreter, a wait-for-definition layer, a hand-written scheduler |
492	| **H, harness** | the per-system harness's own calls (posing stages, requesting answers, printing), which `PROTOCOL.md` fixes before any run |
493	
494	### Rules
495	
496	1. **Reference semantics.** A construct is P if removing it would change the
497	   meaning of the program: for a declarative program, the set of solutions
498	   under the semantics of `SPECIFICATION.md`; for an imperative program,
499	   the values it reports for the queries the problem poses. It is C if
500	   removing it would change only operational behaviour: order,
501	   termination, floundering, errors, efficiency. Where this rule and rule
502	   5 disagree, rule 5 decides.
503	2. A construct that changes both (a red cut, a guard that also orders) is
504	   C, and is listed in the results. But a **guard** that tests only its
505	   case's own head (the pattern or condition the problem's case states) is
506	   P. This is the head test of a committed-choice clause, a pattern match,
507	   or an `if` that dispatches on the case. Only synchronisation or
508	   commitment beyond that is C.
509	3. **Mode-faithful transcription is P.** A function or procedure that
510	   computes exactly the directions the problem's queries use, with one
511	   branch per case of the definition, transcribes the definition. Its case
512	   dispatch (`if not a:`, a match on the head) is P. R covers only:
513	   - arguments or cases the problem does not give;
514	   - a changed algorithm;
515	   - a direction the queries do not use.
516	
517	   So `conc(a, b)` in Python, returning a followed by b by the problem's
518	   two cases, is P for P03a. For P03b, where conc is used to split a
519	   sequence, that function cannot run backwards. A separate splitting
520	   function that keeps conc's meaning on every input used is R, and P03b
521	   is *expressible with reformulation* (`SPECIFICATION.md`,
522	   expressibility). The author has no choice between the two.
523	4. Moving a definition case or a conjunct away from the presentation order
524	   adds no tokens. Each move counts as one move, under reformulation.
525	   Likewise, a guard, case or conjunct of the problem left out of a
526	   program counts as one **omission**, under reformulation. The tokens that
527	   introduce and close the case it is missing from are R. The case's
528	   unchanged contents are classed on their own (rule 10).
529	5. An extra argument added for efficiency is R, even if the program is then
530	   shorter.
531	6. A disjunction or a set of facts that the problem states is P. An
532	   enumeration that the problem does not state is C.
533	7. A comprehension or aggregation construct that states a definition the
534	   problem gives (a set former for setdiff, for instance) is P, the same as
535	   a transcription of the definition by cases.
536	8. Writing an arithmetic relation as an evaluation in one direction is P
537	   where that direction is the one the query uses (rule 3), and R where the
538	   problem needs the relation in a direction the evaluation does not
539	   serve, plus one move if it forces a reordering.
540	9. **Built-ins in place of defined relations.** Using a built-in instead of
541	   a relation the problem defines (memberchk/2 or Python's `in` for mem;
542	   `sum` for sum) is P if it is equivalent in the directions used, and R
543	   otherwise. Either way it is listed, since it may hide the problem's
544	   operations from the step count.
545	10. **Nested constructs.** The tokens that introduce a construct (a loop
546	    header, an if-then-else's condition and connectives) take its class.
547	    The constructs inside it are classed on their own.
548	11. **Declarations that change failure.** A declaration that changes how an
549	    undefined relation behaves (`:- dynamic`, the `unknown` flag) is C, and
550	    is listed, since it chooses a reading of P08.
551	12. A built-in of the configuration's core is counted as its call tokens. A
552	   library outside the core is counted the same way, and is also listed
553	   under external mechanisms. Code written for the experiment is S,
554	   wherever it is kept, counted once per mechanism per configuration. S is
555	   reported apart from the per-problem ratios of C and R to P.
556	13. Code in the harness beyond the fixed harness calls is not H. It is
557	    classed as C or S by these rules, with one exception. **Output
558	    adapters** are H, however long they are: code whose only effect is to
559	    print, or collect for the harness, answers the program has already
560	    computed. That covers a printer that walks an encoded sequence, a
561	    callback that prints an answer, and a stand-in for the fixed harness
562	    calls. Code that computes anything the report depends on is not an
563	    adapter, and nor is code that decides which computation's result is
564	    reported (a test of what is still held, for instance, that chooses
565	    whether to derive the answers another way).
566	14. **A separately written function for a direction** (rule 3) is R
567	    throughout, its case-head tests included. Rule 2's exemption for head
568	    tests applies to transcriptions of the problem's own cases, not to a
569	    function written because a transcription cannot run in that direction.
570	15. **Operations on an encoding are part of the encoding.** Where a systems
571	    file defines an encoding as P, the operations the problem's relations
572	    need on encoded values (construction, decomposition, equality) are P.
573	    A general mechanism beyond the problem's relations, such as a unifier
574	    or a search, is S. Inside a separately written direction function,
575	    rule 14 wins: an encoding operation used only there is R with it.
576	16. **A reset that only lets store be reused** is C, since removing it
577	    changes what is held, not what is computed (rule 1).
578	17. **Docstrings are comments,** and are not tokens.
579	18. In P13, a **native** algorithm is not reformulation (the problem says
580	    so). Its tokens are P. Where a system has only one way to compute a
581	    task, its native and prescribed programs are the same, and are
582	    recorded once, with the prescribed program's classes.
583	19. **Code that holds undecided relations.** In imperative programs for
584	    the staged problems (P01, P02, P05, P07, P09e, P16, among others), code
585	    that holds relations until their values arrive and then decides them
586	    is classed by how general it is:
587	    - written for the problem's own relations, it is R, in the core
588	      configuration;
589	    - general over relations, reusable from one problem to another (a
590	      constraint store, a propagator), it is S, and the program belongs to
591	      the *extended* configuration, named by that mechanism.
592	
593	    Inside such code, each relation's **evaluator** (the function that,
594	    given which of the relation's places are known, decides it, gives an
595	    unknown its value, or waits) is split. *(Clarified after the held-out
596	    check.)*
597	    - Computing any one place from the others, and testing a fully known
598	      relation, is P, in **every** direction the relation has. The problem
599	      states the relation without a direction, and any stage, order or
600	      hidden variant may leave any of its places unknown, so rule 3's
601	      "direction the queries do not use" does not apply here. Which
602	      branches a run happens to reach never decides a class.
603	    - The tests of which places are known, the verdict that the relation
604	      must wait, and what it records about what it waits for, are R: they
605	      are the holding, not the relation.
606	20. **Separators** between two constructs (a comma between arguments, a
607	    semicolon between statements) take the class of the construct that
608	    follows them.
609	
610	### Two classifiers
611	
612	**Calibration.** Before the freeze, programs for P03 and P13 are written in
613	each system of the first comparison, Python and ALGOL 60 included, and both
614	classifiers class them. They are **development examples, not results**.
615	They test whether the rules give consistent classes across different
616	styles of program, where the rules are hardest. The calibration record
617	(`calibration/`) gives:
618	
619	- both classifiers' classes, token by token;
620	- the rate of agreement, per system and per class;
621	- the constructs that caused disagreement;
622	- whether the disagreements fall more on one paradigm than another;
623	- any amendment to the rules that resulted.
624	
625	The first calibration, of draft 0.5, is recorded in
626	[`calibration/README.md`](calibration/README.md). Its disagreements fell
627	almost all on imperative code, and rules 4 and 13–18 come from it.
628	
629	The rules are amended only to make classifications more defensible, never
630	to make the systems' totals come out more alike.
631	
632	Each program is classed independently by two classifiers, who are named,
633	are not the program's author, and are not shown each other's classes. For
634	every token, both classes are kept. Totals are reported per classifier, so
635	that each classifier's classes add up to the same total of tokens, together
636	with the count of disputed tokens and the constructs they belong to. No rule
637	is added after the freeze except by a versioned amendment applied to every
638	system (`PROTOCOL.md`).
639	
640	## The core of a configuration
641	
642	The core is the language as its defining document describes it, for the
643	evidence class of the implementation (`PROTOCOL.md`). Each systems file
644	lists its configurations' cores exactly, built-in by built-in, and the
645	flags that change their meaning. Anything used beyond the core is listed
646	under external mechanisms, even if the implementation ships it.
647	
648	A mechanism a library provides is therefore never counted as native. A
649	twelve-line suspension layer appears as twelve lines' worth of S. A
650	suspension that a library provides appears as an external mechanism.
651	Native suspension appears as neither.
652	
653	## Steps and store
654	
655	Each systems file names, before the freeze, the unit of steps (derivation
656	steps, inferences, reductions), the unit of an alternative, and the unit of
657	store, and how each is measured. They are not chosen afterwards. Wall-clock
658	time is not a metric, with one exception: in P13 only, process CPU time and
659	the operating system's maximum resident set size are recorded as secondary
660	measures of **growth**, since a built-in can do work that no step count
661	sees. They are used only for the growth exponent, never as counts.
662	
663	## Quantities comparable across systems
664	
665	Each system's own units are compared within that system only. Across
666	systems, these quantities are compared, because each problem defines them
667	in its own terms:
668	
669	- **Problem operations.** The applications of each case of each relation
670	  the problem defines. In the prescribed tasks of P13, they are fixed by
671	  the definitions: for example, rev on a sequence of n makes n(n+1)/2
672	  applications of conc's cases beyond those of rev itself. A system that
673	  makes more has done work the problem does not ask for. A program counts
674	  them with counters that are harness code (H), or by instrumentation.
675	- **Problem-defined alternatives.** In P05, the values of x still held. In
676	  P12, the candidates examined (sequences s for which accept(s) is
677	  evaluated) and the partial sequences held, live or kept for
678	  backtracking. In P15a, the interleavings held.
679	- **Growth.** For a problem with a size parameter (P12's n, P13's n,
680	  P16's n), steps, problem operations and each store quantity are fitted,
681	  within each system, by three models: linear (a·n), polynomial (a·nᵏ) and
682	  exponential (a·cⁿ). Each fit is reported, with its residuals, and the
683	  model that fits best is named. The fitted forms and parameters are
684	  compared across systems; the counts are not. P12 is expected to be
685	  exponential for some strategies, and is not forced into a power law.
686	  Three sizes are evidence of how a cost grows over that range. They do
687	  not establish its asymptotic complexity, and no result says they do.
688	
689	## Restart cost and repeated work
690	
691	The two are kept apart. Neither alone establishes how much work was done
692	twice.
693	
694	- **Restart cost**, for a system that cannot receive stage k into its
695	  existing computation, is the step count of running stages 1 to k−1
696	  alone, measured, since those steps are spent again when stages 1 to k are
697	  posed together.
698	- **Repeated work** is counted from a source each systems file names: the
699	  number of times a relation, goal or constraint already examined is
700	  examined again after new information arrives, and the steps those
701	  examinations take. For Absys, the trace. For ALGOL 60, the
702	  `name_repeat_evaluations` count of its measurement build. For SWI-Prolog and
703	  Python, only problem operations counted by the program; the debugger is
704	  not used, because it changes the inference count.
705	- For every stage, both the *incremental cost* (steps from the end of stage
706	  k−1 to the end of stage k, where the system allows it) and the *restated
707	  cost* (steps from nothing to the end of stage k) are recorded beside them.
708	
709	## Intervention
710	
711	An intervention is an action by a person, or by harness code written for one
712	problem, that the fixed harness does not perform. Each is counted per
713	stage:
714	
715	- restarting after an error;
716	- choosing by hand which of several pending computations runs;
717	- reordering the program between stages;
718	- adding a control declaration tailored to one stage.
719	
720	The harness reposing earlier stages automatically, for a system that cannot
721	receive stages incrementally, is not an intervention. It is counted under
722	restart cost.
723

# Problems

| | problem | status in draft 0.5 |
|---|---|---|
| P01–P09 | the original nine | revised after review 1 |
| P10 | [state replacement](10-state-replacement.md) | added after review 1 |
| P11 | [irreversible effects](11-irreversible-effects.md) | added after review 1, reduced, with explicit commitment |
| P12 | [large alternative space](12-large-alternative-space.md) | added after review 1 |
| P13 | [deterministic scale](13-deterministic-scale.md) | added after review 1, prescribed and native |
| P14 | [a process over a message stream](14-message-stream.md) | added after review 1 |
| P15 | [merge and committed choice](15-merge-and-committed-choice.md) | added after review 1 |
| P16 | [shared information at scale](16-shared-information.md) | added after review 2, for concurrent constraint programming's core case |

All sixteen are in the primary suite. P14, P15 and P16 exercise
capabilities that Absys is expected to lack or that other models were
designed for, which is why they are included before any system has been
run. After the freeze, a new problem goes only into a
separate, dated supplementary suite (`PROTOCOL.md`).

## The proposal dropped

**Retries** were proposed under P11 and dropped. The case was an operation
that fails transiently and must be delivered exactly once. It would test a
failure-injecting stub and idempotence, not how partially specified
computations are represented or resolved.
# P04. Unbounded alternative

**Probes:** whether an alternative with no finite derivation stops the
system from finding one that has one, and how the order in which a
recursive definition is written affects its use.

## Vocabulary

loop(x): defined only by

1. loop(x) if loop(x)

Read as the least relation, loop has no instances.

alist(s): s is a finite sequence of the atom ᴀ. Two definitions are given.
They have the same meaning and are written differently.

- **alist-left**, in this order:
  1. alist(s) if alist(m) and s = ⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m, with the two conjuncts in that
     order
  2. alist(⟨⟩)
- **alist-right**, in this order:
  1. alist(⟨⟩)
  2. alist(⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m) if alist(m)

## Queries

Each is one stage.

| | query | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| P04a | loop(x) or x = 1, in that order | x = 1 |
| P04b | x = 1 or loop(x), in that order | x = 1 |
| P04c | alist(⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩), with alist-left | true: one solution, no unknowns |
| P04d | alist(s), with alist-left | infinitely many: s = ⟨⟩, ⟨ᴀ⟩, ⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩, … |
| P04e | alist(⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩), with alist-right | true |
| P04f | alist(s), with alist-right | infinitely many, as P04d |

## Observations

- P04a and P04b: whether x = 1 is reported, and then whether the
  computation finishes, holds alternatives pending, suspends or runs to
  the budget.
- P04c and P04e: the outcome, and whether the computation finishes.
- P04d and P04f: which solutions are reported, in what order, and whether
  every solution would be reached given enough steps. Compare only this
  property across systems, not the number reported within the budget.
# P05. Late contradiction

**Probes:** how a system holds several alternatives while constraints that
eliminate some of them arrive, and what happens to answers it has already
given.

## Vocabulary

pick(x): a closed world of three facts, in this order: pick(1), pick(2),
pick(3).

x > 1 and x ≠ 2 are primitive comparisons.

## P05a. Choice first

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |
| 2 | x > 1 | x ∈ {2, 3} |
| 3 | x ≠ 2 | x = 3 |

## P05b. Constraint first

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x > 1 | every integer x > 1 |
| 2 | pick(x) | x ∈ {2, 3} |

## P05c. Contradiction

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |
| 2 | x = 4 | none |
| 3 | x = 3 | none |

Stage 3 adds to stages that are already inconsistent, so the valid outcome
stays empty.

## Observations

- After each stage: whether every surviving alternative is held at once, or
  one is held and the others kept for backtracking, or the others are lost.
- An answer reported at one stage and invalid at the next: how its
  withdrawal is shown, if at all.
- P05b stage 1: how a comparison on an unknown is treated: held, reported
  as a residual, enumerated, or an error.
- P05c: how the empty outcome is reported, and whether stage 3 can be
  posed at all.

# P06. Negation with unknowns

**Probes:** whether negation gives valid outcomes when the unknowns it
mentions are still unknown, and whether the order of information changes
the outcome.

not R holds of an assignment exactly when R does not hold of it. Definitions
with negation are read under the stratified semantics
(`SPECIFICATION.md`). Relations given by facts are in a closed world.

## P06a. Negation, then a value

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | not (x = 1) | every value x other than 1 |
| 2 | x = 2 | x = 2 |

## P06b. A value, then negation

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x = 2 | x = 2 |
| 2 | not (x = 1) | x = 2 |

## P06c. A contradiction through negation

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | not (x = 1) | every value x other than 1 |
| 2 | x = 1 | none |

## P06d. Set difference

mem(e, s): e is an element of the sequence s. It is defined, in this order,
by:

1. mem(e, ⟨e⟩ ++ t), for every sequence t
2. mem(e, ⟨h⟩ ++ t) if mem(e, t)

setdiff(s1, s2, d): d is the elements of s1 that are not elements of s2, in
their order in s1. It is defined, in this order, by:

1. setdiff(⟨⟩, s2, ⟨⟩)
2. setdiff(⟨h⟩ ++ t, s2, d) if mem(h, s2) and setdiff(t, s2, d)
3. setdiff(⟨h⟩ ++ t, s2, ⟨h⟩ ++ d) if not mem(h, s2) and setdiff(t, s2, d)

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | setdiff(⟨1,2,3,4⟩, ⟨2,4,6⟩, d) | d = ⟨1,3⟩ |

A system with a set-forming construct may state the same definition with it.
That counts as problem tokens too (`METRICS.md`, rule 6).

## P06e. Clark's students

A closed world, from Clark (1978) as rendered by Elcock (1990):

- student(ʙʀᴏᴡɴ), student(ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ)
- maths(ᴄ101), maths(ᴄ301)
- takes(ʙʀᴏᴡɴ, ᴄ101), takes(ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ, ᴄ101), takes(ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ, ᴄ301)

nonmajor(p): p is a student who does not take some maths course. It is
defined by one case:

1. nonmajor(p) if student(p) and maths(k) and not takes(p, k), with the
   conjuncts in that order

| | query | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| P06e1 | nonmajor(ʙʀᴏᴡɴ) | true |
| P06e2 | nonmajor(ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ) | false |
| P06e3 | nonmajor(p) | p = ʙʀᴏᴡɴ |

## Observations

- Whether P06a and P06b give the same outcome. A system that reports no
  solution for P06a is *unsound*; record the step at which the negation
  was decided.
- P06a stage 1: whether the negation is held as a condition, decided at
  once, delayed, or an error. A representation that restricts x to integers
  is *partial*.
- P06e3: whether p and k are known before the negation is decided.
# P07. Simultaneous constraints

**Probes:** which sets of arithmetic relations a system solves, which it
leaves unresolved, and which it gets wrong.

All unknowns are integers. Each set of relations is one stage, in the order
given.

| | relations | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| P07a | x + y + z = 12, y + z = 7, z = 3 | x = 5, y = 4, z = 3 |
| P07b | x + y = 10, x − y = 4 | x = 7, y = 3 |
| P07c | x + y = 10 | every integer pair with x + y = 10 |
| P07d | w · u = v, u = 2, v = 14 | w = 7 |
| P07e | w · u = v, u = 2, v = 15 | none: 15 is not a multiple of 2 |
| P07f | x + y = 10, x + y = 11 | none |
| P07g | x · x = 9 | x = 3 or x = −3 |

P07a is also posed in all six orders of its relations.

## Observations

- For each: the three classifications, with any residual recorded.
- P07e and P07f: whether the inconsistency is detected. A system that holds
  the relations unresolved is *complete* / *residual* / *inconsistency
  undetected*, with *suspended*.
- P07e: a solver over the rationals that reports w = 15/2 is *unsound*
  under this problem's integers.
- P07g: whether both solutions are found.
- What mechanism solves each case that is solved: one relation at a time as
  its values become known, propagation, elimination, or search.
# P08. Late definition

**Probes:** what an application of a relation that has no definition yet
means to a system, and what happens when the definition arrives.

rev and conc are as in P03.

## What an undefined relation can mean

A relation applied before its definition has arrived can be treated as:

1. a relation that is false (it has no instances);
2. a relation whose truth is unknown;
3. a reference to a definition that is unavailable, which is an error;
4. a computation awaiting its definition.

These are different states, and a system may take any of them. Two readings
fix the valid outcomes:

- **closed:** an undefined relation has no instances (state 1);
- **open:** the definition may yet arrive, so an application of it neither
  holds nor fails, and the valid outcomes are those of the other
  information alone.

Neither reading is the valid one. A result records which of the four states
the system takes, and is classified under both readings.

Under the closed reading, a definition's arrival can withdraw an earlier
valid conclusion (no solutions) although the information only grows.
That is the non-monotonicity of conclusions that `SPECIFICATION.md`
describes, and the withdrawal is recorded.

## P08a. A definition that arrives

| stage | information | closed reading | open reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a = ⟨x, y, z⟩ | a = ⟨x, y, z⟩ | the same |
| 2 | rev(a, b) | none | a = ⟨x, y, z⟩; b free; rev(a, b) pending |
| 3 | x = y | none | x = y, a = ⟨y, y, z⟩; b free; pending |
| 4 | the definitions of rev and conc | x = y, a = ⟨y, y, z⟩, b = ⟨z, y, y⟩ | the same |
| 5 | y = z | x = y = z, a = b = ⟨z, z, z⟩ | the same |
| 6 | b = ⟨42⟩ ++ c | x = y = z = 42, a = b = ⟨42, 42, 42⟩, c = ⟨42, 42⟩ | the same |

Under the open reading, before the definition arrives:

- a system that holds rev(a, b) as a pending application, and reports the
  equations, is *complete* / *residual*;
- a system that reports the equations and has silently dropped rev(a, b)
  is also *complete*, with representation *solved form*, and the dropping
  is recorded, since it will lose the application when the definition
  comes;
- a system that reports no solutions is *unsound* under the open reading,
  and *complete* under the closed one.

A declaration that changes how an undefined relation behaves (`:- dynamic`,
the `unknown` flag) is control, and is listed (`METRICS.md`, rule 11).

## P08b. A definition that never arrives

Stages 1 to 3 of P08a, and no more. Record whether the system's report can
be told apart from failure, and which of the four states it shows.

## P08c. A definition that arrives in parts

| stage | information | closed reading | open reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the definition of conc | no unknowns | the same |
| 2 | rev(⟨1, 2⟩, b) | none | b free; pending |
| 3 | rev, case 1 only: rev(⟨⟩, ⟨⟩) | none: case 1 alone does not cover a sequence of two | b free; pending, since case 2 may yet arrive |
| 4 | rev, case 2 | b = ⟨2, 1⟩ | the same |

## Observations

- Which of the four states the system takes, and how a pending application
  is shown.
- Whether stage 4 resumes the pending application, or the application has
  to be posed again (restart cost, or intervention if done by hand).
- P08c: what happens to the application at stage 3. Is it failed, held, or
  resumed with the partial definition? Can stage 4 still reach it?

117	
118	### Mechanisms
119	
120	- **`sys.monitoring`** (PEP 669, 3.12+). A tool registers a callback for

130	`(result, instructions)`. The meter's own frame executes 12 instructions
131	between enabling and disabling the events; the callback ignores the meter's
132	code object, so these are excluded and the count is that of `fn` alone

136

148	sum_loop         100000    700007    700007 True     for x in xs: k += x
149	sorted_builtin   100000         6         6 True     sorted(xs, reverse=True)

153	explicit loops take 16n + 13 and 7n + 7. Summing 10⁵ numbers is 4

164	  Their step counts are not comparable with P13a to P13d, and should be

271

278	
279	### Recommended wording
280	
281	"Python instructions: bytecode instructions executed in Python code
282	(`sys.monitoring` INSTRUCTION events, CPython <version>, all threads), the
283	meter's own frame excluded. Work done inside built-in functions and types
284	is not counted." Exact and deterministic for a fixed version, program and
285	input, with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, and with no iteration over identity-hashed
286	sets or dicts and no threads; otherwise state which of these applies.
287	
288	## 2. Operations the problem defines
289	
290	### Methods compared (p2_algops.py)
291	
292	The probe transcribes range, sum, conc, rev, revacc and racc over cons cells
293	(`()` is ⟨⟩, `(h, t)` is ⟨h⟩ ++ t), runs a P13-shaped workload (build the
294	range, then sum, rev and revacc it), and counts calls to each function four
295	ways. Expected counts, from the definitions: range n + 1, sum n + 1, rev
296	n + 1, conc n(n + 1)/2, revacc 1, racc n + 1.
297	
298	```
299	3.12.2, n=1000 expected {'conc': 500500, 'racc': 1001, 'rev': 1001, 'revacc': 1, 'rng': 1001, 'sm': 1001}
300	  none          result=(500500, 1000, 1000) same=True counts_match=-    cpu=0.024s
301	  A counters    result=(500500, 1000, 1000) same=True counts_match=True cpu=0.062s
302	  B wrappers    result=(500500, 1000, 1000) same=True counts_match=True cpu=0.087s
303	  C monitoring  result=(500500, 1000, 1000) same=True counts_match=True cpu=0.138s
304	  D setprofile  result=(500500, 1000, 1000) same=True counts_match=True cpu=0.200s

306	  none          70112
307	  A counters    124725
308	  B wrappers    152234
309	  C monitoring  70381

315	| method | program text | effect on steps | effect on depth | cost at n = 1000 |
316	|---|---|---|---|---|
317	| A: counters in the functions | one line per counted function | +78% here; grows with every call | none | 2.6× |
318	| B: wrappers bound to the same names | none in the functions; the names are rebound | +117% | one extra frame per call: depth doubles | 3.6× |
319	| C: `sys.monitoring` PY_START, local events on the chosen code objects | none | a fixed setup cost (+269) | none | 5.8× |
320	| D: `sys.setprofile`, filtered by code object | none | a fixed setup cost (+112) | none | 8.3× |
321	
322	All four counts were exact and matched the closed forms on 3.12.2, 3.12.11,
323	3.13.7 and 3.14.6 (B, A and D also on 3.10 and 3.11, which lack C). The
324	results were identical with and without counting.
325	
326	**Least intrusive: C.** It needs no change to the program, adds no frames,
327	leaves the instruction count unchanged apart from its setup, and can run in
328	the same process as the instruction meter (it uses a different tool id).
329	Its cost is paid only on calls to the chosen functions, since the events
330	are enabled on those code objects alone. The harness names the functions to
331	count; that list is H, fixed per problem before any run. Method A puts
332	counting code in the program and inflates the step count, so a program
333	with counters cannot also be the one whose steps are reported. Method B is
334	unsafe for recursive definitions because it doubles the depth.
335	
336	### Making the counts comparable across systems
337	
338	For prescribed-algorithm problems (P13a to P13d), the problem file fixes
339	the definitions, so the number of times each definition is applied is a
340	property of the definition and the input, not of the system. It is the one
341	work figure that can be compared across systems directly. To make it so:
342	
343	1. **Define the unit by the problem.** One *application* of a relation is
344	   one use of one of its cases to reduce a goal or a call: for conc, one
345	   step from conc(⟨h⟩ ++ a, b, ...) to conc(a, b, ...), or one use of the
346	   base case. The closed forms above are then the expected values. For
347	   P13c, rev(⟨1..n⟩) applies rev n + 1 times and conc n(n + 1)/2 times.
348	2. **Count it in each system's own terms, mapped to the unit.** In Python,
349	   one call of the function that transcribes the relation (method C). In
350	   SWI-Prolog, a candidate is the call port of the predicate, which counts
351	   one per goal however many clauses are tried; failed head unifications
352	   are not applications. Each systems file states its mapping.
353	3. **Require transcription as functions.** The count exists only if every
354	   relation the problem defines is a function (a predicate, a procedure)
355	   in the program. If ⟨h⟩ ++ t is written with Python's `+` on lists, there
356	   is no conc call to count, and the work of each concatenation (copying
357	   len(a) + 1 elements) is inside one instruction.
358	4. **Check against the closed form.** A count that differs from the
359	   expected value is a finding about the transcription (an extra case, a
360	   relation computed twice) and should be recorded as such.
361	5. **Report it beside the system's own steps, not instead of them.** The
362	   ratio of steps to applications shows each model's bookkeeping cost per
363	   application, which is what P13 asks for.
364	
365	For problems that do not prescribe an algorithm, such a count exists only
366	where the problem file defines the operation (answers, nodes of a search
367	tree the problem defines). Comparisons and similar operations inside
368	built-ins (`sorted`, `min`, `in` on a list) cannot be counted without
369	replacing the values with instrumented objects, which changes the program;
370	that was not probed.
371	
372	### Recommended wording
373	
374	"Applications of <relation> (calls of its transcribing function, counted by
375	`sys.monitoring` PY_START on that function's code object; no change to the
376	program). Expected from the definition: <closed form>."
377	
378	## 3. Allocated memory
379	
380	### Mechanisms
381	
382	- `tracemalloc.start(nframes)` installs hooks on Python's three allocator
383	  domains (raw, mem, object). `get_traced_memory()` returns `(current,
384	  peak)` in bytes of traced blocks; `reset_peak()` (3.9+) sets the peak to
385	  the current value.
386	- `resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss`: the OS's maximum resident
387	  set size of the process.
388	
389	### Probe (p3_memory.py, 3.12.2)
390	
391	```
392	[outside] mmap of 64 MiB, every page touched
393	  tracemalloc current growth=96 peak growth=216
394	  ru_maxrss before=21020672 after=88064000 growth=67043328
395	[peak] build and drop 10^6 ints inside a call
396	  current growth=84 peak growth=40000208
397	[ints/strings] lists of 100000 elements kept (current growth, bytes)
398	  keep_small_ints  current=   800960 peak=   801064 per_element=8.0
399	  keep_large_ints  current=  4000960 peak=  4001032 per_element=40.0
400	  keep_same_obj    current=   800032 peak=   800040 per_element=8.0
401	  keep_const_str   current=   800960 peak=   801064 per_element=8.0
402	  keep_built_str   current=  5392960 peak=  5393096 per_element=53.9
403	[freelist] 10^5 floats created and freed one at a time
404	  current growth=32 peak growth=152
405	[maxrss of a child process] keep_large_ints(10^6), tracemalloc off/on
406	  off maxrss growth=39960576 traced_peak=0        tracemalloc_own=624
407	  on  maxrss growth=118685696 traced_peak=40449336 tracemalloc_own=48777968
408	[steps] instructions of keep_large_ints(10^4), tracemalloc off/on
409	  off=70012 on=70012
410	```
411	
412	The tracemalloc figures were identical in three runs (md5 of the output
413	without the rss and timing lines) and the same on 3.13.7 except
414	`keep_small_ints` (800,928). 3.10.15 reported a traced peak of 36,449,500
415	for the 10⁶ build against 40,449,336 on 3.11+.
416	
417	### What tracemalloc sees
418	
419	- **A true peak.** The peak is updated on every allocation: a 10⁶-element
420	  list built and freed inside a call left a peak of 40,000,208 bytes (8 for
421	  the pointer and 32 for each int), with current memory back to 84. No
422	  sampling is involved.
423	- **Only allocations through Python's allocators, after `start()`.** A
424	  64 MiB anonymous `mmap`, every page touched, was 96 bytes in tracemalloc
425	  (the mmap object) and 67 MB in `ru_maxrss`. C libraries that call
426	  `malloc` directly are likewise invisible. Allocations made before
427	  `start()` are not traced, and their frees are ignored; start it with
428	  `-X tracemalloc` to trace from interpreter start-up.
429	- **Shared objects cost nothing.** Small ints (−5 to 256), `None`, and a
430	  constant string are shared: a list of 10⁵ of them costs 8 bytes per
431	  element, the list's own pointers. 10⁵ distinct ints cost 40 bytes each,
432	  distinct short strings 54. A count of "elements held" and a count of
433	  bytes therefore disagree depending on the values.
434	- **Free lists.** 10⁵ floats created and freed one at a time showed 32
435	  bytes of growth: the interpreter reuses freed objects, and objects kept on
436	  a free list remain traced.
437	- **Requested sizes only.** tracemalloc counts the sizes requested, not
438	  pymalloc's arena and pool overhead or fragmentation. That is documented
439	  behaviour; it was not separately probed.
440	
441	### Overhead
442	
443	- CPU: building 10⁶ ints took 7 to 16 times as long with tracemalloc on
444	  (1 frame), and 24 to 220 times with 25 frames, depending on the version
445	  and the run.
446	- Memory: tracemalloc's own tables held 48,777,968 bytes for 10⁶ live
447	  traced blocks, about 49 bytes per block, and the child's `ru_maxrss`
448	  growth went from 40 MB to 119 MB. With tracemalloc on, `ru_maxrss`
449	  measures tracemalloc as much as the program.
450	- Steps: none. The instruction count was the same with it on and off.
451	
452	### `ru_maxrss`
453	
454	A true peak of resident memory for the whole process: interpreter, loaded
455	modules, allocator arenas, mmaps, and tracemalloc if on. About 16 to 21 MB
456	at start on these builds. It never decreases, so within one process only the
457	first stage's peak can be read unless the stage starts above every earlier
458	peak; one process per measured stage is needed. The unit is bytes on macOS
459	and KiB on Linux (the Linux unit is documented, not checked here). Resident
460	size also depends on the OS's paging, so it is a measurement of the run,
461	not of the program.
462	
463	### Recommended wording
464	
465	"Traced memory, current and peak (bytes, `tracemalloc`, 1 frame, started
466	before the stage, peak reset at the stage start): memory requested through
467	Python's allocators. Excludes allocator overhead and memory allocated
468	outside Python's allocators." Exact for what it covers; the peak is a true
469	peak. Separately, if needed: "process maximum resident set size
470	(`ru_maxrss`, one process per stage, tracemalloc off)", labelled a
471	whole-process peak.
472	
473	## 4. Retained logical state
474	
475	Python has no store of suspended goals or choicepoints of its own. What a
476	computation holds is in the program's own objects. The probes
477	(p4_retained.py) looked at what can be counted at an observation point.
478	
479	```
480	[stack] dfs_bits(k): answers, peak length of the program's stack
481	  k= 4 (16, 5)   k= 8 (256, 9)   k=16 (65536, 17)
482	[gens] bits(k) suspended after its first answer
483	  k=16 live generators (gc)=17 chain via f_locals=1 chain via gc.get_referents=17
484	  after del: 0
485	[gcobjs] which objects gc.get_objects() lists
486	  int 10**9 False; str False; tuple of ints False; tuple holding a list True;
487	  list True; dict of str->int False (True on 3.14.6); cons cell (1, ()) False
488	[blocks] sys.getallocatedblocks() around keeping 10^4 cons cells
489	  before=63442 kept=83443 (+20001) after del=63444 (+2)
490	```
491	
492	- **The program's own structure.** The length of an explicit stack,
493	  queue, frontier or agenda is exact at any point the program or harness
494	  can reach it. A peak exists only if the program records it as it goes,
495	  which is code in the program: harness-class (H) if the harness interface
496	  fixes it, otherwise classed by the token rules. The figure counts
497	  entries, and what an entry stands for depends on the program (a pending
498	  branch, a partial solution), so the structure is named with the count.
499	- **Suspended generators.** A nested generator suspended after its first
500	  answer holds one frame per level: 17 for depth 16, found by filtering
501	  `gc.get_objects()` for generators with a live `gi_frame`, after
502	  `gc.collect()`. Following the program's own references from the outer
503	  generator also gives 17 through `gc.get_referents()` on 3.11+ (it gave 1
504	  on 3.10.15). It does not work through `gi_frame.f_locals`, since a
505	  suspended `for` keeps its iterator on the value stack, not in a local.
506	  The `gc` scan costs time proportional to the heap and runs a collection;
507	  use it only at observation points.
508	- **`gc.get_objects()` is not an object count.** It lists only
509	  GC-tracked objects. Ints, strings, tuples of atoms (including cons cells
510	  whose tail is an atom-only tuple, after a collection untracks them) and,
511	  before 3.14, dicts of atoms are not listed. A count of retained cons
512	  cells cannot be had from it.
513	- **`sys.getallocatedblocks()`** counts live allocator blocks: keeping
514	  10⁴ cons cells with distinct int heads added 20,001 blocks (10⁴ tuples,
515	  10⁴ ints, 1 other), and freeing them returned to +2. Differences were
516	  the same in every run and version; the absolute value varied by a few
517	  dozen between runs. It is a usable count of objects retained, in blocks,
518	  but it includes interpreter-internal blocks and is shared by all threads.
519	- **Frame depth** at a point: walking `sys._getframe().f_back` (2 at top
520	  level of the probe, 53 inside 50 nested calls). Exact.
521	
522	### Recommended wording
523	
524	"Retained alternatives: entries in the program's <stack / queue / frontier
525	of …> (count at <point>; peak recorded by harness code)." "Suspended
526	generators: generator frames not finished, `gc.get_objects()` after
527	`gc.collect()`, at <point>." "Live allocator blocks (`sys.getallocatedblocks()`
528	difference from stage start)." Never "objects" for `gc.get_objects()`.
